Side Chamber
SYDE CHAYM-ber
n. (one of the storied chambers built against the wall of the temple)
Hebrew tsela, a rib, a side, and thence a side chamber; the chambers were ribs along the flank of the house. Named in the Authorized Version in Ezekiel's temple vision.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The side chambers were small rooms built in three storeys against the outer wall of the house of the LORD, running round it on every side except the front. Solomon built them: “And against the wall of the house he built chambers round about, against the walls of the house round about, both of the temple and of the oracle: and he made chambers round about” (1 Kings 6:5). Ezekiel measures them in his vision of the restored house: “After he measured the wall of the house, six cubits; and the breadth of every side chamber, four cubits, round about the house on every side” (Ezekiel 41:5), and then notes their arrangement, three one over another and thirty in order. The construction detail carries the point. The beams of the chambers rested on ledges cut into the temple wall, which narrowed as it rose, so that the chambers leaned on the house without being let into it: “that they might have hold, but they had not hold in the wall of the house” (Ezekiel 41:6). Nothing pierced the sanctuary. The chambers served for storing tithes, vessels, and the priests' portions, and for the priests' use when they came off duty. They are the ordinary offices of the house, leaning on the holy place and never intruding into it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Side chamber, one of the small rooms built in three stories against the outer wall of the temple, resting on ledges in the wall but not let into it, used for stores and for the priests.

Hebrew tsela, a rib, a side, and thence a side chamber.

Built in three stories against the wall of the house, 1 Kings 6:5-6.

Thirty in order, three one above another, Ezekiel 41:6.

Four cubits broad, resting on ledges in the narrowing wall.

Used for tithes, vessels, and the priests' chambers, Ezekiel 42:13-14.

Key Scripture

1Ki 6:5 — "And against the wall of the house he built chambers round about, against the walls of the house round about, both of the temple and of the oracle: and he made chambers round about:"

Eze 41:5 — "After he measured the wall of the house, six cubits; and the breadth of every side chamber, four cubits, round about the house on every side."

Eze 41:6 — "And the side chambers were three, one over another, and thirty in order; and they entered into the wall which was of the house for the side chambers round about, that they might have hold, but they had not hold in the wall of the house."

Eze 44:19 — "And when they go forth into the utter court, even into the utter court to the people, they shall put off their garments wherein they ministered, and lay them in the holy chambers, and they shall put on other garments; and they shall not sanctify the people with their garments."

Modern Corruption

Scripture's building measurements are dismissed as tedious filler; the construction of the side chambers is itself a doctrine of reverence.

expand to see more

The common treatment of these chapters is to skip them. Ezekiel 40 through 42 and 1 Kings 6 are counted among the dull places of the Bible, useful to architects and nobody else, and the reader who skips them loses a lesson the Holy Ghost thought worth cubits and courses to teach. The chambers lean on the house; they do not breach it. Everything useful, administrative and ordinary in the service of God was arranged so that it touched the sanctuary without penetrating it. That is a working definition of reverence, and it was built in stone before it was ever stated in a proposition.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives the pattern of His own worship down to the ledges in a wall. The regulative principle is not a Puritan invention imposed on a silent Bible; it is the plain inference from a God who measured the side chambers. Where Scripture has spoken about His house, men are not free to improve on it, and where it has not spoken, they are not free to add.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsela, a rib or side; the storied chambers built against the temple wall.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsela, a rib, a side, hence a side chamber.

The same word is used of Adam's rib in Genesis 2:21-22.

Built in three stories, thirty in order, Ezekiel 41:6.

Resting on ledges in a wall that narrowed as it rose, 1 Kings 6:6.

Called also the chambers of the house and the holy chambers.
